name: Ahasbai
title: Father of Elifelet, one of David's thirty heroes
summary: In the list of King David's chosen mighty men in 2 Sam 23:34, Ahasbai from Maakat appears as the father of Eliphelet. Although he plays no independent role in the biblical narratives, his connection to Maakat – a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee – sheds light on the geographical and ethnic breadth of David's elite guard. That a family's roots lay in an area that was sometimes at conflict with Israel (cf. 2 Sam 10:6-8) underscores that David's circle of heroes was shaped by personal loyalty and military skill rather than narrow tribal affiliation. The parallel list of mighty men in 1 Chr 11:35 contains variant name forms, which testifies to complex manuscript traditions in the transmission of these texts.
roles: father of one of David's heroes

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as the father of Elifelet in David's list of heroes
keyEvents.description: Ahasbai from Maakat is mentioned as the father of Elifelet in the list of David's thirty mighty warriors. His son Elifelet was part of this select group, a position that testifies to outstanding military skill and loyalty to King David.

keyEvents.title: Parallel list of heroes in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: A parallel list of David's heroes is found in 1 Chronicles. Here the son is named 'Eliphal, son of Ur', showing textual variations between the two lists. Such differences reflect different manuscript traditions and copying practices in antiquity.

versions.summary: Ahasbai from Maakat is mentioned in the Bible as the father of Elifelet, one of King David's thirty mighty warriors. He is known only through his son's service among David's elite soldiers. His name preserves the memory of a family that served faithfully in David's kingdom.
versions.title: Father of one of David's heroes
versions.reason: [major] Ahasbai is not himself described as a warrior in the Bible. He is only mentioned as the father of Elifelet. There is no biblical basis for attributing to him the role 'warrior'. A more appropriate role would be 'father of one of David's mighty men' or similar.; [minor] The second key event includes verses 34–39, but most of these verses concern other heroes, not specifically Elifelet. It would be more precise to limit the reference to verse 34.; [minor] The third key event (the establishment of David's mighty men) concerns the three mightiest heroes and is not directly linked to Ahasbai. This event is general and adds little specific detail to Ahasbai's profile.; [major] In 1 Chr 11 there is a parallel list of David's mighty men, but Ahasbai's name does not appear directly there. In Chronicles the name 'Uri' (or variants) is used instead of Ahasbai, and the son is called Eliphal, not Elifelet. The reference should be clarified, and the description should mention the name variations.; [minor] The summary is well phrased, but the sentence 'His name preserves the memory of a family that served faithfully in David's kingdom' is somewhat speculative. It could be improved by staying closer to the biblical text.; [minor] The ID 'elifelet' is reasonable, but note that in 1 Chr 11:35 the son is called 'Eliphal' rather than 'Elifelet'. This can be mentioned as a name variant, but for consistency with 2 Sam 23:34, 'elifelet' is acceptable.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. Notes should be added regarding the linguistic aspect of the name Ahasbai, the name variations between the books of Samuel and Chronicles, and the geographical connection to Maacah.

versions.title: Father of Elifelet, one of David's thirty heroes
versions.reason: [minor] The second key event (Eliphelet serving among David's elite soldiers) overlaps strongly with the first event, as both refer to the same verse (2 Sam 23:34). It adds limited value to have two separate events pointing to exactly the same verse. One might consider merging them or differentiating their content more clearly.; [minor] The scripture reference to 1 Chr 11:35-36 should be verified more closely. In some traditions, only verse 35 is the relevant parallel, but including verse 36 may be reasonable depending on how the passage is bounded. This is a minor uncertainty.; [minor] The summary is good, but the phrasing "mentioned in the Bible" is somewhat redundant in the context of a biblical person profile. It could be tightened.

versions.summary: Ahasbai from Maakat is known as the father of Eliphelet, one of King David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Sam 23:34). He is not mentioned independently in the biblical texts but is known solely through his son's place among David's elite soldiers. The connection to Maakat, a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee, suggests that the family may have originated outside Israel's core regions. This illustrates the broad, cross-cultural recruitment for David's band of heroes, which included warriors from various ethnic groups and regions.
versions.title: Father of Elifelet, one of David's thirty heroes
versions.reason: [minor] In 1 Chr 11:35-36 there is some uncertainty about whether the verses are correct as a parallel to Elifelet/Elifal. Traditionally, 'Elifal son of Ur' is mentioned in verse 35, not 35-36. Verse 36 contains another name. However, this depends on the verse division in different textual traditions, so this is a marginal note.; [minor] The summary is very similar to the two previous versions, especially the opening phrase 'Ahasbai from Maakat is known as the father of Elifelet, one of King David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Sam 23:34)'. Since there are already two earlier versions with a similar introduction, the text should vary more to avoid repetition.

footnotes.text: The name Ahasbai (Hebrew: אֲחַסְבַּי) has an uncertain etymology but may mean 'I have sought refuge' or be derived from a root meaning 'to flee'. The name appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (2 Sam 23:34), making it a so-called hapax legomenon among biblical personal names.

Maakat (or Maakah) was a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee, in the border region toward Golan. In 2 Sam 10:6-8, Maakat is mentioned as one of David's opponents in war, which makes it all the more remarkable that a man from this area had a son among David's elite warriors. This illustrates how David's heroic guard included warriors from various geographical and ethnic backgrounds.

There are striking differences between the lists of mighty men in 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11. In 2 Sam 23:34, 'Eliphelet son of Ahai from Maacah' is mentioned, while the parallel text in 1 Chron 11:35-36 has 'Eliphal son of Ur'. Such textual variations likely reflect different manuscript traditions and copying practices over time, and they are an important area of study within Old Testament textual criticism.

David's thirty mighty men (Hebrew: שְׁלֹשִׁים, sheloshim) formed an elite group of warriors who served as David's personal guard and military leaders. The list in 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11 actually contains more than thirty names, which may be due to new members being added over time as some fell in battle, or because the title was an institutional designation rather than an exact number.

The area of Maacah is also known from other Old Testament texts. In Josh 13:13 it is noted that the Israelites did not drive out the inhabitants of Geshur and Maacah, and the people there continued to live among the Israelites. This provides background for how individuals connected with Maacah could become integrated into Israelite society.
